questions.stem: Which multiplication has the same answer as 3 + 3?
questions.stemText: Which multiplication has the same answer as 3 + 3 ?
questions.explain: Count the 3s: there are 2 of them, so this is 2 groups of 3, which is 2 × 3 = 6. Counting one group too few gives 1 × 3, which is 3 too little, and multiplying the wrong pair gives 3 × 3 or 1 × 2. Multiplication is a short way of writing the same number added over and over - that is the whole idea, and it is why the times tables are worth knowing by heart.

questions.stem: Aisyah works out 5181 + 1292 in columns. One column makes 17, so she writes 7 in that column and a small 1 above the column on its left. How much is that small 1 worth?
questions.stemText: Aisyah works out 5181 + 1292 in columns. One column makes 17, so she writes 7 in that column and a small 1 above the column on its left. How much is that small 1 worth?
questions.explain: The column that makes 17 is the tens column: 8 + 9 = 17, and no other column reaches ten. 17 tens is 1 hundred and 7 tens, so the 7 stays in the tens column - worth 70 - and the small 1 goes above the hundreds column - worth 100. The small 1 is worth 100. A mark is worth the column it is written in, not the digit it looks like: that is what regrouping means, ten of something small becoming one of the next size up. Every wrong answer here is one of the two slips - the right digit read in the wrong column, or the wrong digit read in the right one.

questions.stem: Jun Hao works out 51 + 55 in his head. He makes 60 first. 51 + 55 = 60 + ?
questions.stemText: Jun Hao works out 51 + 55 in his head. He makes 60 first. 51 + 55 = 60 + ?
questions.explain: To get from 51 up to 60 you need 9, so 9 is moved across from the 55. That leaves 55 − 9 = 46, and 60 + 46 = 106. Whatever you give to one number you must take off the other, or the total changes. You could have rounded the 55 up to 60 instead and taken that amount off the 51: it is the same total either way, so it lands on the same answer.

• The ones digit is 4 more than the tens digit.
• The hundreds digit is 8.

questions.stemText: Kavitha is thinking of a 3-digit number. These are her clues: • The ones digit is 4 more than the tens digit. • The hundreds digit is 8. • It is an even number. What is the greatest number it can be?
questions.explain: Write down the digits you are told: the hundreds digit is 8. The ones digit is 4 more than the tens digit, so list every pair that works: tens 0 and ones 4; tens 1 and ones 5; tens 2 and ones 6; tens 3 and ones 7; tens 4 and ones 8; tens 5 and ones 9. (With tens 6, the ones digit would be 10, which is not a digit.) So the number could be 804, 815, 826, 837, 848 or 859. It is even, so its ones digit must be even: cross out 815, 837 and 859. That leaves 804, 826 and 848. The greatest of these is 848. (Without the last step you would choose 859, but it breaks the clue “It is an even number.”)

questions.stem: At the school bookshop, boxes of crayons cost $4 each, or 4 for $13. Siti needs 10 boxes of crayons. What is the least amount Siti must pay? (in dollars, e.g. 4.75)
questions.stemText: At the school bookshop, boxes of crayons cost $4 each, or 4 for $13. Siti needs 10 boxes of crayons. What is the least amount Siti must pay? (in dollars, e.g. 4.75)
questions.explain: Buying 4 boxes of crayons one by one costs 4 × $4 = $16, but 4 for $13 is cheaper, so buy as many bundles as you can. 10 ÷ 4 = 2 remainder 2, so 2 bundles cost 2 × $13 = $26. The 2 boxes of crayons left over cost 2 × $4 = $8 (cheaper than one more bundle at $13). Total: $26 + $8 = $34. Buying all 10 one by one would cost $40.

questions.explain: Each square side is 32 ÷ 4 = 8 cm. The 4 squares together: 4 × 4 × 8 = 128 cm. The rectangle: 32 + 8 + 32 + 8 = 80 cm. Difference: 128 − 80 = 48 cm. Shortcut: each of the 3 cuts makes 2 new sides of 8 cm, and 3 × 2 × 8 = 48 cm.
